10765-thrilling-adventures-by-land-and-s:
James O. Brayman edited Thrilling Adventures by Land and Sea as a book of remarkable historical facts gathered from authentic sources. Its preface defends true adventure against cheap, harmful fiction, arguing that readers who seek amusement deserve stories that also inform. Flood and field supply its motto, borrowed from Othello's tale of moving accidents.

The volume collects escapes, wrecks, battles, and survivals, chosen for excitement and truth together. Brayman's aim is wholesome thrill, not sensation for its own sake. Readers get a sturdy anthology of real-life adventure, in the taste of an earlier age of popular history.
10849-saved-at-sea:
Mrs. O. F. Walton wrote Saved at Sea as a lighthouse story for young readers. Its hero is born on a stormy day when waves beat the lighthouse rock and wind rages against all within. His grandfather, keeper of the light, had never known such a storm since coming to live on the rock. Chapters follow a flare at sea, a bundle saved, and little Timpey.

The tale moves through fog, waiting boats, a change of light, and a new neighbor, toward the claiming of the Sunbeam. Walton writes with Christian warmth and seaside detail. Children get adventure and faith together, in a story that made Walton a favorite of Victorian nurseries.
11058-jack-archer-a-tale-of-the-crimea:
G. A. Henty wrote this boys' adventure about Jack Archer, a midshipman in the Crimean War. Jack begins at the King's School, Canterbury, where term starts dull after holidays, then sails to Gibraltar, Gallipoli, and the Crimea. Battles at the Alma, Balaklava, and Inkerman, a great storm, and the siege of Sebastopol follow, with chapters on prisoners, escapes in disguise, and Polish insurgents.

Jack is taken prisoner, held on parole, and escapes, while a Russian count's daughter, Katinka, and court intrigues add romance to the war story. Henty writes with his usual energy for schoolboys, mixing history with heroics. The novel gives young readers a vivid, if dated, view of the Crimean War through one boy's service.
12150-north-south-and-over-the-sea:
M. E. Francis, Mrs. Francis Blundell, gathered these stories in 1902 for the Country Life Library of Fiction, with illustrations by H. M. Brock. Several had appeared before in the Cornhill Magazine, Longman Magazine, and Country Life.

The book divides into three parts. North holds Lancashire and Yorkshire tales like Golden Sally and The Conquest of Radical Ted. South holds village romances, and Over the Sea holds Irish and emigrant stories. Francis writes in dialect and local color, favoring plain folk, stubborn lovers, and small moral turns. The stories suit readers who like regional England and Ireland rendered with affection and a light comic touch.
12173-the-two-lovers-of-heaven-chrysanth:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translated Calderon drama The Two Lovers of Heaven from Spanish in 1870, with dedicatory sonnets to Longfellow and others. Calderon, the great dramatist of Counter-Reformation Spain, set the play in early Christian Rome.

Chrysanthus, a young Roman noble, converts to Christianity and falls in love with Daria, a vestal virgin who shares his faith. Pagan priests, family pressure, and imperial law drive the lovers toward martyrdom, and the motto Por la fe morire, for the faith welcome death, frames their choice. Mac-Carthy verse keeps Calderon baroque imagery and theological argument. The play offers English readers a rare taste of Spanish Golden Age drama in full.
12483-reminiscences-of-scottish-life-cha:
This 1874 volume, twenty-second edition enlarged, gathers reminiscences of Scottish life and character by Dean E. B. Ramsay of Edinburgh, with a memoir by Cosmo Innes. Friends, publishers and relatives asked Innes to write the memoir, giving him authentic facts, dates and the dean's own views.

Chapters cover Scottish religious feeling, old conviviality, domestic servants, judges, humour from Scottish expressions and proverbs, and stories of wit. Ramsay's anecdotes preserve a Scotland of kirk, court and household talk, fondly recalled. The book is a classic of Scottish social memory, humorous, affectionate and rich in dialect colour.
13367-hills-and-the-sea:
Hilaire Belloc writes of walking, sailing, and looking at old places in a work of travel and reflection. He dedicates it to Philip Kershaw, the other man of a pair who loved each other like brothers yet quarrelled on nearly all things. One of the Faith and the other certainly not.

Belloc reads walls built in a fashion forgotten since the Antonines, watches Rome fall asleep as sculpture loses power. He finds a Pyrenean valley fit for camping, fishing, and walking up all the way. Hills and sea become a way to think about history, faith, and friendship. The prose moves between guidebook detail and a walker's sudden, personal judgment.
13518-the-journey-to-the-polar-sea:
Sir John Franklin's Journey to the Polar Sea tells of an overland Arctic expedition in simple, faithful prose, praised in its introduction for revealing the character of its writer. Mr. Beck misses his ship at Yarmouth and rejoins her at Stromness after nine successive days of travel, a small sign of the hardships and changes that fill the narrative.

Guides sketch the Copper-Mine River on the floor and name the Copper Indians who know its lower course to the sea. Hunters follow animal tracks north to a strait, keep deer skulls from dogs and wolves by hanging them in trees, and live by rules learned from the land. Franklin's account remains a classic of Arctic travel, plain in style and rich in northern detail.
1354-chronicles-of-avonlea:
L. M. Montgomery returns to Avonlea, the Prince Edward Island village of Anne of Green Gables, for short stories of its people. Her subjects are lovers, gossips, old maids, and children, each with a small drama of pride, love, or forgiveness. Anne herself appears at the edges, now grown.

Montgomery writes the island with warmth and humor, and her tales are gentle, romantic, and full of local color. The book suits readers who loved Anne and want more of her village, in stories that stand on their own. Montgomery's Avonlea tales still welcome readers back to the island.
1407-a-message-from-the-sea:
Set in a steep Cornish fishing village, this Christmas story opens with the arrival of Captain Jorgan, a bluff American sailor. He brings talk of the sea and a message that stirs an old local sorrow. A young villager long thought lost may still be alive, and a family must face hope it had buried.

Told in short chapters, the tale moves between the cliff village, the shore, and the ships that link it to the wider world. It mixes humour, sea lore, and feeling, and ends with a homecoming of sorts. It is a gentle seasonal story about news long delayed and ties renewed.
14352-patty-and-azalea:
Carolyn Wells wrote this 1919 Patty book, a light novel of family life and house parties. Patty, now a mother, keeps house with her husband Bill and their small daughter Fleurette. Guests stream in from New York for weekends of talk, meals, and fun. Into this cheerful house comes Azalea, a new relative whose odd manners upset the household. The tale is told with warmth, jokes, and a keen eye for social gaffes.

Patty frets that Azalea cannot be made to blend, like a figure against its background. At dinner Azalea yawns openly across the flowers, and the family calls her queer. Yet Azalea gets her chance, and a sampler, a picture play, and a house party all shape her story. Philip Van Reypen and other friends drift through the weekend fun. The novel charms as a sunny tale of manners, kin, and second chances.
14432-a-dream-of-the-north-sea:
James Runciman's 1889 book describes the lives of North Sea fishermen and the mission work that reached them aboard smacks and in port towns. Runciman knew the fleet from earlier reporting, and he writes with sympathy for men at sea.

Chapters follow storms, long voyages, drink, gambling, and the preaching and confession meetings that offered an alternative fellowship. The title points to a vision of a kinder, more hopeful life for sailors. The book blends reportage, sermon, and sea story, and it helped raise support for missions to deep-sea fishermen. Its portraits of hardship aboard the smacks remain vivid.
14832-a-maid-of-the-silver-sea:
John Oxenham's romance, partly written on a verandah at Sark looking toward France, follows Nance, a maid of the silver sea. Two lie in a cleft, Nance comes to be herself, and a new mine captain arrives, while Gard makes new acquaintances and shines through modest veiling.

Grannie schemes schemes, Gard fights gales and Tom, Tom wants to but does not dare, and old Tom finds a silver heart. Oxenham writes island life with warmth: sea, mines, families and courtship in a Channel Island world. Dedicated to Edward Baker of La Chaumiere, Sark, the novel is a gentle love story set where land, sea and silver meet.
15411-a-voyage-to-the-south-sea:
William Bligh published this account in London in 1792, by permission of the Admiralty, with charts. The voyage had a royal order behind it: carry the breadfruit tree to the West Indies in His Majesty's ship Bounty, under Bligh's command. The title page promises the full story, including the mutiny and the open-boat voyage that followed.

Chapters trace the plan, the outfit, and the sailing from England, with stops at Tenerife, the Cape of Good Hope, Van Diemen's Land, and the Pacific islands. After the mutiny, part of the crew sailed in the ship's boat from Tofoa to Timor, a Dutch settlement in the East Indies. Bligh's narrative, written to correct a hasty first account, remains the classic firsthand record of the Bounty affair.
15420-broken-homes-a-study-of-family-des:
Joanna C. Colcord, superintendent of New York's Charity Organization Society, published this social work study in 1919 for the Russell Sage Foundation. It asks why men desert their families, and how charities should answer. A district secretary's line opens the argument: before the deserter, there was a broken man, bankrupt for the time in health, hopes, or prospects.

Chapters move from causes to treatment: finding the missing husband, gathering facts, and shaping help case by case. Colcord also treats the home-staying non-supporter, and closes with next steps in corrective and preventive work. The book is practical, not sentimental, drawing on case records to show what aid could and could not do. It remains a clear record of early social work facing family breakdown.
16142-the-communist-threat-in-the-taiwan:
Released by the State Department in September 1958, this pamphlet gathers official American papers on the Taiwan Straits crisis. It prints Secretary Dulles's statement of September 4, a White House statement, President Eisenhower's report to the American people, and Eisenhower's letter to Premier Khrushchev. The series number is Far Eastern Series 76.

Dulles states that Taiwan, Quemoy, and Matsu had never been under Communist authority, remaining under Free China since the Second World War, and that the United States stood bound by treaty. The pamphlet lets readers follow Washington's public case during artillery attacks on the offshore islands. It remains a compact primary source on Cold War Asia.
16243-journal-of-landsborough-s-expediti:
William Landsborough's journal, published in Melbourne in 1862 by F. F. Bailliere, records his expedition from Carpentaria in search of Burke and Wills. Anxiety for the lost explorers raised four parties within a short time: Howitt from Melbourne, McKinlay from Adelaide, Walker from Rockhampton, and Landsborough from Brisbane. The steamer Victoria, under Commander Norman, sailed to the Gulf of Carpentaria to support them.

Landsborough's route, shown on a map, crosses the Gulf country toward the interior, through heat, flood, and rough ground. His daily entries give the search its human scale, with horses, stores, and native guides. Readers of Australian exploration will find a plain, gripping record of a famous rescue quest.
16347-miscellanea:
Juliana Horatia Ewing's Miscellanea, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, gathers papers republished to complete her collected works. The preface admits the pieces were not republished in her lifetime, a sign she did not rate them highly, yet each holds a special interest that justifies bringing them forward. Ewing's gift for mimicry shapes the book, since she acted above the average of amateurs and could imitate any style she wished.

The first four stories show that mimic power at work, copying other voices with wit and accuracy. Later pieces add sketches, verses, and odds and ends from a busy writing life. Readers who know Ewing's children's classics will enjoy these slighter, revealing extras.
16936-parker-s-second-reader-national-se:
Richard G. Parker, principal of the North Johnson School in Boston, wrote this second reader in the National Series of selections for reading, adapted to the standing of the pupil, issued by A. S. Barnes and Burr in New York in 1851. Part second is designed for younger classes in schools and academies. A motto from Acts asks, understandest thou what thou readest.

Parker gathers short prose and verse for young readers, graded to their level, with lessons in reading, morals, and knowledge. The book served thousands of American schoolrooms. Modern readers get a clear window on 1851 schooling, and teachers of reading history will find a useful, plain sample of how children once learned to read aloud.
17480-the-digger-movement-in-the-days-of:
Lewis H. Berens, author of Towards the Light, published this study of the Digger movement in London in 1906 with Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company. He dedicates it to the Society of Friends, whose doctrines he learned to love while writing. The subtitle calls Gerrard Winstanley, the Digger, a mystic and rationalist, a communist, and a social reformer.

Chapters run from the Reformation in Germany and England, through the great civil war, to the Diggers themselves. Winstanley, his exposition of Quaker doctrines, the new law of righteousness, and the Diggers' manifestoes follow. Readers get a careful history of England's first communist movement, drawn from Winstanley's own writings.
17694-adventures-in-new-guinea:
James Chalmers of Port Moresby wrote this account of adventures in New Guinea, published in London in 1886 by the Religious Tract Society, with six pictures. Chalmers notes that public attention had lately turned to New Guinea, whose name often appeared in newspapers and missionary reports. His introduction sets the scene for a missionary's travels among coastal peoples.

Readers get a Victorian missionary adventure, mixing exploration, encounter, and evangelism in the Pacific. The book suits readers of mission history and of New Guinea's colonial past. Its Tract Society origin marks its earnest, improving tone.
17910-the-mafulu-mountain-people-of-brit:
Robert W. Williamson wrote The Mafulu Mountain People of British New Guinea in 1912, printed in London by Macmillan, with a preface by A. C. Haddon. Williamson studied a mountain folk of Papua, then little known to outsiders, and he gives their life in full, careful detail.

The book covers homes, dress, food, rites, law, and trade, with pictures and a map to aid the reader. Haddon, a famed anthropologist, lends his name to the work. It is a classic early ethnography, written with the era's colonial gaze, and it stays a key source for the Mafulu, best read with modern Papuan studies at hand.
18062-stories-of-ships-and-the-sea:
Jack London wrote these Stories of Ships and the Sea, printed as Little Blue Book number 1169 in Girard, Kansas, by Haldeman-Julius. The copyright stands in the name of Charmian London, his widow, and the set was reprinted by arrangement for cheap, wide sale.

Five tales fill the book: Chris Farrington, able seaman, a typhoon off Japan, a lost poacher, the banks of the Sacramento, and a stay in Yeddo Bay. Chris, a lad of seventeen, spars with a Swedish sailor over rank and manners. The stories are brisk, salty, and full of sea life, a fine pocket sample of London at his best.
18268-ballads-of-lost-haven-a-book-of-th:
Bliss Carman, author of Low Tide on Grand Pre and Songs from Vagabondia, published this book of sea ballads at Boston in 1897. Lamson, Wolffe and Company issued the volume, printed at the Norwood Press. Carman writes of sailors, ships, and shore towns, with the sea as both workplace and fate.

Contents open with A Son of the Sea, whose speaker was born for deep-sea faring and bred to put to sea on stories of his father's daring. Later ballads give The Gravedigger, The Yule Guest, The Marring of Malyn, The Nancy's Pride, Arnold master of the Scud, and The Ships of St. John. Legends of Lost Haven, The Shadow Boatswain, and The Last Watch close the set. Readers get sea poetry in ballad form: storms, legends, and the pull of the tide.
1861-an-old-town-by-the-sea:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich's Old Town by the Sea is a portrait of Portsmouth, New Hampshire, sung first through the Piscataqua River, which sings by gleaming isles, woods, and fields of corn. Aldrich, writing from a city and full of vague unrest, looks back to the town of his boyhood with affection.

The sketches walk the reader past great houses with oaks and elms, tessellated marble walks, and small square buildings abutting the street. They dwell on the town's sea captains and old families. The book is a gentle work of local memory, and it remains a charming introduction to a New England port before it changed.
1880-the-pathfinder-or-the-inland-sea:
Natty Bumppo, older now, works as a guide on Lake Ontario — the inland sea of the title — where forest war meets naval war. Cooper's preface explains the plan: to join seamen and savages in incidents that might be supposed to happen on the great lakes, where forest war meets naval war.

The tale follows Pathfinder's love for Mabel Dunham, a young woman who has come to the frontier, and his rivalry with officers and Indians alike. Cooper writes the lake country with the care of a man who knew it. The novel's set pieces — canoes, storms, and night attacks — give it the shape of the Leatherstocking Tales at their most adventurous.
1958-hermann-and-dorothea:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's Hermann and Dorothea, is a verse epic of German village life. It follows Hermann, a young man who falls in love with Dorothea, a refugee girl fleeing the French Revolution. The poem is set in a small town on the Rhine, where war arrives as a column of wagons on the road.

Goethe writes the story in hexameters, giving a village romance the dignity of epic. The poem's fame rests on its balance: love and war, home and exile, held in a single, calm narrative. It remains one of Goethe's most loved works, and a good entry point to his poetry for readers new to it.
19993-childhood-s-favorites-and-fairy-st:
Childhood's Favorites and Fairy Stories is a young folks' treasury of classic tales. Its contributors' list reads like a hall of fame. Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus, appears there. Franklin K. Lane, the Interior Secretary, lends his name. Ernest Ingersoll the naturalist writes for the young here too. The Hamilton Wright Mabie circle edited the treasury in 1909. Famous pens were gathered to stock one family volume.

Treasuries like this decided which stories counted as childhood's favorites. Fairy tales, animal stories, and poems fill the big book. Editors promised parents the best, pre-selected and safe. The famous-contributor list was the selling point and the standard. Many American childhoods were furnished from such volumes. This one shows the canon being packaged.
20190-the-handy-cyclopedia-of-things-wor:
The Handy Cyclopedia of Things Worth Knowing is a manual of ready reference for daily use. Its pages define hard words and give brief facts in strict order. Copperas is ferrous sulfate, one short entry tells the reader plainly. Diathesis means a bodily bent toward a certain kind of illness.

Other entries cover fines, pay for office, and Greek myth alike. Erebus is the dark region the dead cross toward Hades. Such handbooks put a small library on one shelf for busy homes. Readers get a quaint, handy store of the facts its era prized most.
21087-the-ghost-ship-a-mystery-of-the-se:
John Conroy Hutcheson's mystery of the sea opens at a blazing sunset aboard the ocean steamer Star of the North. The weather has looked threatening all day. Soon the officers face a puzzle that pulls the tale in and out of the supernatural.

Again and again the ship meets the same vessel sailing in a direction that seems impossible. Her officers check their position and grow more baffled each time. Hutcheson grounds the mystery in daily life aboard a late nineteenth-century steamer, with its watches, routines, and weather. Readers get a ghost story tested against charts, compasses, and hard-headed sailors.
21088-the-white-squall-a-story-of-the-sa:
Tom is thirteen, and his father is a naval officer on half pay who has bought property in the West Indies. John Conroy Hutcheson sends the boy home to school in England after an accident delays his start. A ship's captain takes charge of him for the voyage.

That voyage brings nearly every mishap a sailing ship could meet. A white squall, a sudden line squall, strikes and capsizes the vessel in the Sargasso Sea. Tom and the crew must right her and carry on to England. Hutcheson wrote the tale as a lively first guide to ships for young readers.
21104-afloat-at-last-a-sailor-boy-s-log-:
Allan Graham, a country vicar's son, signs on as an apprentice aboard the Silver Queen at Wapping Docks for a voyage to Shanghai. Irish bosun Tim Rooney takes to the lad and teaches him the ropes. John Conroy Hutcheson logs the ship warping out of dock and down the Thames under a steam tug.

Seasickness in the Bay of Biscay, a stowaway in the forepeak, and friendship with the Chinese cook Ching Wang fill the outward run. Past the Cape of Good Hope, Malay pirates trail the ship through typhoon weather. She grounds on the Pratas shoal before the voyage ends.
21301-bunyip-land-a-story-of-adventure-i:
Joe Carstairs works on an Australian farm, poring over maps, in George Manville Fenn's New Guinea adventure. His father, a keen naturalist, set off years before to collect specimens in New Guinea and was never heard of again. Joe plans a search expedition, taking a local doctor and an Aboriginal worker from the farm.

A stowaway, Jimmy, joins them with his dog Gyp. In New Guinea they hire porters and push inland, finding Joe's father held prisoner with another Englishman whose mind has broken under captivity. Fenn supplies the usual close shaves, strange creatures, and jungle dangers before the party brings the lost men home.
21366-sail-ho-a-boy-at-sea:
Alison Dale is seventeen and already a practised yachtsman from his father's boats. He ships out on his first real cruise in George Manville Fenn's later sea tale. His skipper is an unpleasant man, and the crew holds worse: a half-French troublemaker named Jarette leads a mutiny. The ship is taken, and officers and passengers are cut off from her.

Most of the loyal party are cast adrift to die, with two of their number left aboard. Rescuers return for them just as the drunken mutineers set the vessel afire and flee. A fight for the burning ship follows, with Jarette at its centre until the end.
21367-sappers-and-miners-the-flood-benea:
George Manville Fenn sets one of his tensest tales in Cornwall. Its scene is an old tin mine whose workings run far out beneath the sea. Colonel Pendarve's son Gwyn starts the book at breakfast, hungry from dawn work by the boats. The mine may date to Roman or even Phoenician tin traders.

Fifty-two chapters give Fenn room for his chapter-end perils, and the flood beneath the sea of the subtitle hangs over every descent. Boys, miners, and old workings meet in passages where one wrong step brings the Atlantic in. Fenn's transcriber called it among his very best, and the underground setting makes the suspense tighter than his open-sea tales.
21373-syd-belton-the-boy-who-would-not-g:
Sydney Belton dines with his father, a naval captain, and his uncle, an admiral, and disappoints them both: he does not want the navy. Rounds with the local doctor have turned his head toward medicine. George Manville Fenn sets the tale in the mid-eighteenth century, cocked hats and all, with France as the coming enemy.

Syd runs away with the gardener's son, comes home, and finds his mind changed toward the sea after all. His father's old connections reach the First Sea Lord himself, and the outcome gives Captain Belton command of the Sirius. The boy who would not go to sea becomes the title's joke and its lesson.
21392-happy-jack-and-other-tales-of-the-:
Happy Jack, and Other Tales of the Sea gathers sea stories by W. H. G. Kingston. The title tale opens on the Naiad, a small brig working the run between London and Leith. Her young narrator joins her at about fourteen, in far from grand style.

Kingston paints shipboard life in plain detail, from the dark forecastle to the captain's cabin. Leaks, pumps, watches, and rough weather shape each day at sea. The tales that follow share that close feel for work aboard sailing craft. For readers who want the daily grind and risk of the old merchant sea, the set is rich fare.
21403-the-pirate-of-the-mediterranean-a-:
Malta opens the scene of W. H. G. Kingston's long sea novel The Pirate of the Mediterranean. Kingston praises the island's fine climate, bright skies, and deep store of history. From there the tale moves out over the eastern seas.

A Greek pirate preys on Italian, Greek, and Turkish ships in those waters. Kingston builds the chase through tense scenes and narrow escapes at sea. The book runs long, some nineteen hours read aloud, and it earns its length. Readers who want Barbary corsairs should note this pirate is a different foe. The craft, coasts, and crews are drawn with Kingston's usual care.
21450-ben-burton-born-and-bred-at-sea:
Ben Burton is born to a sailor's wife in W. H. G. Kingston's Ben Burton, or Born and Bred at Sea. His father Dick, a quartermaster of the old Boreas, comes home wounded from a cutting-out raid. News of the baby greets him as he climbs the ship's side.

The tale follows Ben from birth to senior naval rank through a string of sea and shore scenes. A drifting dinghy brings an ayah and a small white girl into the tale. She grows up alongside Ben, spared his hardest fights. Years fly fast, as they do in such tales, and incident crowds upon incident.
21717-battles-with-the-sea:
Lifeboat crews are the heroes of this Ballantyne book, which frames their work as a war that never ends. The foe is the sea itself, which strikes without warning and takes hundreds of lives each year. Against it stand the men of the lifeboats and rocket crews, ready day and night to launch into storms.

Ballantyne tells true-style tales of wrecks, rescues, and brave deeds along the British coast. He wrote the book so boys would know this quiet war and honor those who fight it. The chapters mix stirring sea stories with plain facts about how rescues were made and what they cost.
21761-synopsis-of-some-genera-of-the-lar:
Fungi with names few readers will know fill this slim scientific pamphlet by C. G. Lloyd, printed at Cincinnati in January 1917. Lloyd works over three groups of large pyrenomycetes: Camillea, Thamnomyces, and Engleromyces. A fine specimen of Camillea Cyclops, sent by the Reverend Torrend from Brazil, set the study going. Photographs taken in European museums back the text.

Lloyd argues that the known species can be told apart from good figures, even without close study of their structure. He warns that many tropical finds now filed under other names are really Camilleas. The work is dry, exact, and meant for specialists. It shows the careful sorting work behind every tidy shelf of natural history.
22056-the-mountain-that-was-god-being-a-:
John H. Williams called his 1905 volume The Mountain That Was God, a little book about the great peak of the Northwest. The mountain is Rainier, the huge extinct volcano that rules the skyline near Tacoma and Seattle. Native peoples had treated the white summit as a god. Williams set out to show it from every side.

Glaciers, forests, and climbing routes all enter his account. He compares the text to a glacial river, narrow but swift, running through grand scenery. Photographs and sketches support the words. The book helped turn Rainier from a distant landmark into a place Americans wanted to visit and protect.
22275-vc-a-chronicle-of-castle-barfield-:
V.C., published by David Christie Murray in 1904, joins Castle Barfield to the Crimean War. Murray opens on a stormy night above his fictional parish. Darkness brings one sign of cheer: the lights of the grey-stone mansion on Beacon Hill. Window after window glows until the whole house seems charged with warmth, while the tempest pours its strength against the walls.

From that house a hero goes to the Crimea, where the Victoria Cross was born. Murray, who had reported wars himself, writes battle with a correspondent's eye. The home parish and the trenches test the same men. The novel is a late-Victorian tribute to the V.C. and the villages that bred its winners.
23271-sunk-at-sea:
Sunk at Sea follows castaways who build a new life after a wreck. In time they return to a village, where a mission is set up. A small church with a spire goes up, and that spire soon proves its worth in a moment of danger.

Another vessel calls for water. Its crew would have fired on the settlement out of spite. Seeing the spire, the crew restrain themselves. The heroes then persuade the captain to take them aboard, though Will now loves the missionary's daughter. Readers get shipwreck, mission work, and romance, with a sequel promised in a companion tale.
23273-john-deane-of-nottingham-historic-:
John Deane of Nottingham tells the historic adventures, by land and sea, of a real Nottingham man. After service in Russia, Deane became British consul at Ostend. He held that post for many years before returning home to honours in his native town.

Deane was made a burgess of Nottingham and settled in the nearby village of Wilford. There he died in 1760. His tomb stands there beside his beloved wife Elizabeth's, in the quiet churchyard. Readers get a true-life adventure: a sailor and soldier whose travels ended in office, honour, and a marked grave.
2765-the-lady-from-the-sea:
Henrik Ibsen wrote this play about Ellida Wangel, a lighthouse keeper's daughter married to Dr. Wangel, a widower in a small Norwegian fjord town. Ellida loves the sea with a longing her husband cannot share, and she waits for a stranger from her past.

The Stranger, a sailor to whom she once bound herself, returns to claim her, and Ellida must choose freely between husband and sea. Ibsen writes with symbolic power about marriage, freedom, and the pull of wild nature. The play endures as a haunting study of a woman choosing her own life.
4544-the-cell-of-self-knowledge-seven-ea:
Edmund G. Gardner edited this collection of seven early English mystical treatises, first printed by Henry Pepwell in 1521 and reissued with an introduction and notes in 1910. The opening work, called Benjamin, comes from Richard of Saint Victor, and it traces how dread, sorrow, hope, love, and other powers of the soul rise toward true contemplation. Other pieces draw on Saint Catherine of Siena and on Margery Kempe.

Further treatises include Walter Hilton on the song of angels, an epistle of prayer, and kindred short works on the inner life. Together they show how medieval English writers pictured self-knowledge as a cell, or quiet room, where a person learns their own nothingness and God's goodness. Readers get a scholarly doorway into medieval devotion, with old texts made readable for modern study.
47-anne-of-avonlea:
Anne Shirley becomes Avonlea's schoolteacher in this sequel to Green Gables. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Avonlea finds Anne at sixteen, teaching, keeping house, and raising twins. Marilla adopts Davy and Dora, a lively pair.

Schoolroom mishaps, an irate neighbor, and Miss Lavendar's romance fill the chapters. Anne's ideals meet the daily work of duty and patience. Gilbert Blythe's friendship deepens through the year. The book keeps Anne's humor while she steps toward adulthood. The Avonlea books together trace Anne from orphan arrival to teacher, friend, and young woman of purpose.
5221-the-satyricon-volume-04-escape-by-s:
This fourth volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's translation, follows Encolpius, Giton, and Eumolpus as they escape by sea. From chapter ninety-nine onward, the fugitives board ship, quarrel, scheme, and face shipwreck and new dangers, carrying the picaresque adventures of the Roman novel into its maritime episodes.

The volume contains only this stretch of the story, not the whole Satyricon, and its bracket code marks later additions and forgeries woven into the text. Readers following the novel in order will find here its sea-borne middle passage, told with the same mix of low comedy and literary parody.
5340-further-chronicles-of-avonlea:
L. M. Montgomery's Further Chronicles of Avonlea gathers more tales of the village that was home to Anne of Green Gables. Its stories include Aunt Cynthia, The Materializing of Cecil, David Spencer's Daughter, Jane's Baby, The Failure of Robert Monroe, The Return of Hester. The Little Brown Book of Miss Emily appears among them.

Later tales follow Sara's Way, The Son of Thyra Carewe, The Education of Betty, The Selflessness of Eunice Carr, The Dream-Child, and finally Tannis of the Flats. Readers return to Avonlea's personalities and events in a warm companion volume, told with Montgomery's humour and affection for Prince Edward Island life.
596-rivers-to-the-sea:
Sara Teasdale gathers poems of city, sea, and war in this volume, in five parts. Spring night, Broadway, a Woolworth tower at night, and a subway station open the book; Indian summer, the sea wind, and the carpenter's shop follow. Later parts hold songs overseas and a closing sequence on Sappho.

Teasdale writes in short, musical lines, with images of fog, light, and water. Love, longing, and the sea recur, never dressed in heavy show. The book marks her growth from love songs to a wider world, where a park at night can hold as much feeling as a lover's face.
6041-stories-by-english-authors-the-sea:
Sea stories fill this volume, headed by W. Clark Russell's extraordinary adventure of a chief mate. Newspapers of 1876 reprinted a merchantman's log. The ship Hercules of Liverpool reported a volcanic island hove up in the North Atlantic, while chief officer Michael Balfour fell overboard and vanished despite a boat lowered within fifteen minutes.

Sir Walter Besant's Quarantine Island, the Rock Scorpions, the master of the Chrystolite, Petrel and the Black Swan, Grant Allen's Melissa's Tour, and Vanderdecken's message home complete the set. The tales mix wreck, quarantine, and ghostly messages, all told in the salt air of the merchant service.
6255-there-is-sorrow-on-the-sea:
A letter dated York Factory, Hudson's Bay, 23rd September 1747, opens this tale, addressed to a dear cousin Fanny. A year before, on April Fool's Day, the writer left her on the sands at Mablethorpe. He swore she would never see or hear from him again. Coast guards flashed their lights over the sands that night. One stumbled and dropped his lantern, and in the dark the cousins stole apart, she homeward with a whispered blessing.

Parker tells the rest through memory, as the writer, lonely in the far north, lives the bad night over bit by bit and tries to work it out. Distance brings a clearer sight of old games played in the sand and choices that cannot be undone. It is a short, sad tale of parting, told in a letter's voice, where sorrow sits on the sea between two people who once knew each other well.
653-the-chimes-a-goblin-story-of-some-be:
Charles Dickens writes a New Year goblin tale in this Christmas book, where bells ring an old year out and a new year in. The story opens with a warning that few people would care to sleep in a church at night, alone, while the wind moans round the pillars and tries the doors. Toby Veck, a poor porter, hears the chimes and meets their spirits.

Dickens writes with warm, urgent prose, full of winter wind, organ notes, and moral fire. The tale argues that the poor deserve hope, not blame. It endures as a beloved Christmas story, where bells teach a man to trust the future he feared.
6622-legends-that-every-child-should-kno:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edits a set of great legends for young people, with pictures by Blanche Ostertag and Guy, Earl of Warwick, on the cover. His introduction starts with words themselves, noting how they grew slowly from human need, not made to order like parts of a machine. That slow growth, he says, shows the brotherhood of men.

The legends that follow span times and lands, chosen for wonder, courage, and moral force. Mabie keeps the telling clear for young readers, without dulling the tales. Legends That Every Child Should Know is a solid, old-style gift book, made to start a child on the great stories of the world.
6847-cytherea:
Joseph Hergesheimer opens Cytherea with Lee Randon on a shorn hill, playing what he thinks is his last golf of the year. Country spreads in sere tones to a grey horizon, a stream holds a cold glimmer in frost-killed grass, and wind scatters soft crystals of snow. Alone, with no boy to carry clubs, Lee recalls a refusal by Peyton Morris, who married his niece and is fourteen years younger.

At worse than forty-five, Lee feels age and desire pull against each other, and a woman named Cytherea enters his life. Hergesheimer writes with a novelist's eye for mood and manners. Cytherea is a polished, adult novel of love, age, and longing in the 1920s.
6993-the-lord-of-the-sea:
M P Shiel's Lord of the Sea runs through forty seven chapters of exodus, hunting crops, meteors, guns, and ships of steel. Early chapters name the Fez, a swoon, Reid's, Pearson's Weekly, and the elm, before Hogarth's guns and Isaac set a harder note. Wroxham Broad, the rose, and a priest lead to a monsignor, a rope, old Tom's letter, and chloroform, with a great bell and an infirmary.

Later chapters bring the deep, a meteorite seen by Frankl, church building, a bag of light, and a claim of priority. Hammers, wonder, reefs of steel, the Kaiser, and a cup of trembling precede the Boodah and the battleships, the straits, and a manifesto. A wedding, a visit, a land bill, a regency, and Estrella the prophetess close a vast romantic saga.
769-the-book-of-tea:
Kakuzo Okakura wrote this short book on tea as an art of life in Japan. He traces tea from its origins in China to the Japanese tea ceremony, where a bowl of tea becomes a rite of harmony, respect, and quiet beauty. The chapters move from the history of the leaf to the cult of tea and its place in art.

Okakura argues that the West, with its noise and haste, has much to learn from the tea room's calm. His prose is lyrical and aphoristic, full of contrasts between East and West. The book, first written in English, remains a beloved introduction to Japanese aesthetics, and to the idea that small acts can hold deep meaning.
7784-from-the-lips-of-the-sea:
Clinton Scollard's From the Lips of the Sea gathers sea lyrics that urge the reader to sit alone by the shore and listen. The opening sonnet promises Eddas of old kings, runes of forgotten lore, and solemn secrets of infinity trembling on the sea's dark lips, for those who hearken well.

Contents move from sea marvels, mist, and dirge for a sailor to bagpipes at sea, wild geese, a sea change, and night song by the water. Dawn, lilac seas, summer shores, and moonrise follow in turn. It is a book of music and mood, where the ocean speaks in rhythm and image.
7831-when-london-burned-a-story-of-resto:
G. A. Henty's When London Burned, a story of Restoration times and the Great Fire, defends Charles II's reign against a charge of mere disgrace. Court waste and vice, he admits, helped doom the Stuarts, yet trade and wealth grew fast, and sailors under York, Albemarle, Rupert, and Sandwich fought as bravely as under Blake.

Their wins took naval and commercial lead from Holland, even as plague and fire struck London hard. Through a boy's eyes amid court, plague, and flame, Henty tells how a battered nation still advanced, and how ordinary courage met disaster in the streets of a burning capital.
7957-out-of-the-fog-a-story-of-the-sea:
C. K. Ober wrote this short sea story with a foreword by Dr Wilfred T. Grenfell, who had spent twenty years working along the Labrador coast. Grenfell introduces the tale as a record worth preserving, tied to his own efforts to improve charts and sailing directions for those dangerous waters. The narrative belongs to the world of coastal boats, fog, and hard weather off Labrador.

The story is brief and direct, told as a seaman's experience rather than a grand adventure. Its value lies in its setting: a coast where fog could strand a crew and where Grenfell's mission work tried to bring help. Readers who enjoy true-seeming tales of the sea will find a compact, atmospheric account of life and risk on the North Atlantic shore.
7974-the-pilot-a-tale-of-the-sea:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this sea tale around a mysterious pilot who guides American ships along a hostile coast during the Revolutionary War. Dedicated to his naval friend William Branford Shubrick, the novel draws on Cooper's own seafaring experience and on the daring raids of John Paul Jones, whose figure stands behind the pilot. Storms, chases, and shore parties drive the action.

Cooper, who had already proved himself on land with the Leatherstocking tales, here proved he could write the sea with equal force. The pilot himself, secretive and commanding, remains one of his most memorable creations. Readers who enjoy naval adventure will find the book a founding example of the genre in American literature.
8255-the-world-english-bible-web-hosea:
Hosea was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ, and his book turns his own marriage into a parable. At God's command he married a woman who was unfaithful to him. He used that broken marriage to picture Israel's unfaithfulness, a people chasing other gods while still claiming God's love. The pain in the book is personal as well as prophetic.

Short oracles of judgment alternate with sudden outbursts of tenderness, as God refuses to give up the people he calls his child. Hosea's images of a husband, a father, and a farmer have shaped how later writers speak of love betrayed and renewed. It is a short book, fierce and heartbroken in equal measure.
8396-the-gentleman-a-romance-of-the-sea:
Alfred Ollivant, author of Bob, Son of Battle, sets this sea romance in July 1805, in the age of Nelson. Contents open with the death of Black Diamond. They follow the man on the grey, the galloping gent, the gunner of the sloop, and old Ding-Dong, through a tale of the navy in wartime. The gentleman of the title moves through a world of ships, guns, and honor.

Ollivant writes for readers who love sea stories with strong characters and period color. The 1908 novel belongs to the tradition of naval romance, where duty and daring test a man. Readers get action at sea and a hero shaped by the navy he serves, in a story told with warmth for its service.
9826-homeward-bound-or-the-chase-a-tale-:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote Homeward Bound, or The Chase, a tale of the sea and of American society. His preface explains the plan: fresh arrivals from Europe, meeting America at Sandy Hook, would see the nation's traits with sharper eyes. The tale was to open at the country's threshold and follow the travellers inward. Cooper, famed for sea and frontier tales, steers this voyage himself.

The chase of the title drives the plot across the Atlantic, as shipboard folk debate manners, politics, and home. Cooper writes with a sailor's knowledge and a critic's eye. A reader gets a lively Cooper novel, where a sea voyage becomes a mirror of young America.
994-riders-to-the-sea:
On a bare island off the west coast of Ireland, an old mother waits for news of her sons, who make their living from the sea. One by one the waves have taken them, and now her last two boys ride out to face the same tide. J. M. Synge built this short play from the speech and life of the Aran islanders.

Maurya, the mother, moves from dread to a grim calm as each loss lands, and her final words accept what no prayer could change. The sea itself acts as a force no one can bargain with. In under an hour of stage time, the play packs grief, faith, and the hard terms of island life.
a-message-from-the-sea:
Charles Dickens opens his Christmas tale in a Cornish fishing village built straight up a cliff, where Captain Jorgan marvels at the steep streets. A bottle found at sea carries a message that stirs old grief in the village. The story appeared in the Christmas Stories collection, in the 1894 Chapman and Hall edition used here.

Chapters named The Village, The Money, and The Restitution carry the plot from discovery to repayment of a long-hidden wrong. Dickens wrote the tale with Wilkie Collins for a Christmas number, and it mixes sea weather, village talk, and a family secret. It reads as a warm, compact piece of holiday storytelling.
an-old-town-by-the-sea:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich writes about Portsmouth, New Hampshire, the old seaport where he was a boy. He opens with a poem to the Piscataqua River, longing for its shores from a city desk. The contents promise Captain John Smith, strolls about town, old Strawberry Bank, and personal reminiscences.

Aldrich walks the reader past wharves, gardens, and old houses, pausing for the sailors, merchants, and odd characters who filled them. He tells the town's story from the first sassafras hunters of 1603 onward, in graceful, unhurried prose. The book is both a small history and a love letter, preserving a New England port as steam and rail were changing it.
anne-of-avonlea:
Lucy Maud Montgomery's sequel follows Anne Shirley at sixteen, now the schoolteacher of Avonlea, the Prince Edward Island village where she grew up. The contents list thirty chapters. Anne helps found a village improvement society, teaches a classroom of strong personalities, and looks after neighbors old and young with her usual mix of energy and daydreaming.

Marilla, her guardian, takes in young twins Davy and Dora, and Davy's mischief drives much of the comedy. Anne also coaxes along the shy romance of Miss Lavendar, a lonely woman in a stone house, whose lost love returns by the final chapters. The book ends with a wedding at that house and Anne ready for college. It is gentler and more communal than the first Anne book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acacius-bisho:
Acacius, Bishop of Beroea, was born in Syria about 322, dying about 432. While still very young he joined the solitaries' community under Asterius just outside Antioch. He proved a fervent champion of orthodoxy through the Arian troubles, suffering greatly for his courage and constancy. When Eusebius of Samosata returned from exile after Valens's death in 378, he ordained Acacius to the see of Beroea.

Acacius next appears in Rome as deputy for Meletius and the Antiochene synod when Apollinaris's heresy came before Pope Damasus. He signed the Two Natures profession of faith, and his efforts helped end the schisms at Antioch. He later attended the second general council at Constantinople in 381, joined the illegitimate consecration of Flavian, and died at the remarkable age of one hundred and ten.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-cae:
Andrew of Caesarea was Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. Krumbacher assigns him to the first half of the sixth century, though others place him anywhere from the fifth to the ninth century. Almost nothing else is known of his life. His principal work is a commentary on the Apocalypse, printed in Migne's Patrologia Graeca, volume 106, columns 215 to 458.

The commentary matters because it is the oldest surviving commentary on the book, and most later commentators drew on it. The writer knows early patristic literature far more widely than most Byzantine commentators. Later writers drew on it heavily, so it preserves earlier tradition as well as offering its own reading of Revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arethas-of-ca:
Arethas of Caesarea was born at Patrae in Greece about 860 and was a disciple of Photius like all eminent men of his time. He became archbishop of Caesarea in the early tenth century and ranks among the most learned theologians of the Greek church. He compiled the oldest surviving Greek commentary, or scholia, on the Apocalypse, the Book of Revelation, drawing heavily on his predecessor Andrew of Caesarea. It first appeared in print in 1535 as an appendix to Oecumenius's works.

Through his interest in earliest Christian literature, caught perhaps from Andrew, we owe the Arethas Codex, Paris Greek 451. Through it the writings of the Greek Christian apologists have largely reached us. He also commented on Plato and Lucian, and the famous Plato manuscript called Codex Clarkianus, carried from Patmos to London, was copied by his order. The entry presents a scholar whose copying saved ancient texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurea:
Aurea, meaning golden, was a title given to certain famed works and documents, listed here as five. First comes the Golden Bull, the charter of Emperor Charles IV. It fixed the law of future imperial elections on 10 January 1356, in union with the estates of the empire. Next is the Catena Aurea, a chain of Scriptural commentaries gathered by St Thomas Aquinas. Third is the Legenda Aurea, a collection of saints' lives by Jacopo da Voragine, Archbishop of Genoa.

Fourth is the Summa Hostiensis, also called the Summa of the Archbishop. It expounds the chief parts of Gregory IX's Decretals, by Henricus de Segusio, Cardinal of Ostia, who died in 1271. Last is the Tabula Aurea, an index to Aquinas's Summa Theologica prepared by Pietro da Bergamo. The entry gives no more than these identifications, yet the five titles together sketch a golden shelf of medieval law, Scripture study, and saints' lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bagnorea:
Bagnorea, anciently Novempagi or Balneum Regium, is a diocese in the Viterbo district of Italy. It answers immediately to the Holy See, and its city holds about 4,500 people in a diocese of 20,000. Tradition says St Ansanus preached there in the third century, and a church outside the Alban Gate marks his prison. No record dates the diocese, but Gregory the Great attests Deacon John as bishop about the year 600.

Montefiascone belonged to Bagnorea until Urban V made it a separate diocese, and an alleged 1449 union with Viterbo lacks proof. Its churches include an ancient Gothic cathedral and a new one built by Bishop Nardi in 1698. It preserves an arm of St Bonaventure, a citizen of the town, with some of his writings. Barbarian Goths and Lombards took the city often between the sixth and ninth centuries, and Louis I joined it to the Papal States in 822.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balanaea:
Balanaea was a titular see of Syria, a city founded as a colony of Aradus. Stephanus places it in Phoenicia, though it belongs rather to Syria. Its first known bishop attended Nicaea in 325, and three more are known to the sixth century. It then served as suffragan of Apamea, metropolis of Syria Secunda. When Justinian built the province of Theodorias, Balanaea joined it civilly yet stayed under Apamea in church matters.

By the tenth century it stood exempt, directly under the Patriarch of Antioch. Crusaders raised a Latin see there, known about 1200, and its bishop lived at Margat, a Hospitaller castle. Franks called it Valania and Muslims Bulunvoas, and its river marked Jerusalem's border with Antioch. Today Banias is a village of about 1,550 people, mostly Maronites, growing onions, olives, and fine tobacco.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basil-of-amas:
Basil of Amasea, or Basileus, was a bishop and martyr of Pontus. Jerome's Eusebius text puts his death under Licinius, in AD 321 to 324. His name appears among bishops at Ancyra and Neo-Caesarea in 314. Eusebius records Licinius's cruelty at Amasea, where rulers gave bishops the pains of crooks.

Athanasius counts the great Basileus of Pontus among bishops holding the Son of like substance with the Father. Philostorgius's tale that Basileus went to Nicaea must be wrong, since Nicaea's lists name Eutychianus of Amasea. His Acts, said to be by the eyewitness priest Johannes, are false and wholly fabled. His feast falls on 26 April in Greek and Roman books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beroea:
Beroea, a titular see of Macedonia, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. It lies at the foot of Mount Bermios, now called Veria by Greeks, and still keeps its ancient name. Rome took it after the battle of Pydna in 168 BC, and Pompey wintered there in 49 to 48 BC.

Its Jewish synagogue heard St. Paul preach with success, and on leaving he left Silas and Timothy behind. Onesimus, once the slave of Philemon, counts as its first bishop in the Apostolic Constitutions. The entry joins classical geography to apostolic memory in a short note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarea:
Caesarea in Cappadocia began as Mazaka, named for the legendary hero Mosoch, and later took the name Eusebeia, then Caesarea, named for Tiberius when Cappadocia became a Roman province in A.D. 17. It stayed the metropolis of Cappadocia Prima and the first metropolis of the Patriarchate of Constantinople. Bishops listed from the first to the eighteenth century number fifty, among them Saint Basil the Great and Firmilian, correspondent of Saint Cyprian.

Its saints include the whole family of Saint Basil and the martyrs Mamas, Gordius, and Julitta, praised by Basil himself. Councils met there in 314, 358, and 371, and at Basil's time the diocese counted fifty country bishops. Today it is Kaisarieh in Turkey, with about 72,000 people, Greek, Armenian, and Muslim, and ruins of the old city a quarter mile west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canea: Canea once served as a titular see of Crete, until a decree of 1894 suppressed it. Canea is the Italian name of Cydonia. The two names were used at the same time as separate titles. Cydonia, the Greek name, and Canea, the Italian name, thus stood side by side as two titles for one Cretan see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corea:
Gustave Mutel's entry covers Corea, a vicariate apostolic coextensive with the Empire of Corea, created distinct in 1831. For nearly half a century before, Corea held fervent Catholics. In a manner perhaps unique in Church annals, the Faith arrived without preaching, before any missionaries had penetrated the country. Educated people, eager for new knowledge as their country closed jealously, procured through the annual Peking embassy every possible book on science, literature, and other subjects.

Some Christian books reached their hands, and, grace aiding, they recognized the truth. One, Ni-seung-houn, journeyed to Peking in 1784 and was baptized there as Peter. Returning, he baptized his learned, high-placed companions. Persecution broke out in 1839, with many Christians arrested, tortured, and killed, and missionaries hunted without mercy. The Kang-hoa expedition, avenging murdered French missionaries, lacked vigour. 1907 statistics list one bishop, 46 French missionaries, ten Corean priests, eleven French sisters, 41 Corean sisters, and 72 schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dead-sea:
A geographical entry describes the Dead Sea, the lake on Palestine's south-eastern border, known by many biblical names. The Old Testament calls it the Salt Sea, the Sea of the Arabah, and the East Sea. Josephus and Pliny called it the Lake of Asphalt, and local people call it Bahr Lut, the Sea of Lot. Only once does the Old Testament use its present name.

The Dead Sea ends the Jordan valley's chain of waters. The chain runs from Mount Hermon through Lake Merom and the Lake of Tiberias. Travellers compare the Dead Sea to Lake Geneva in size and shape. It is forty-seven miles long, about ten miles wide, and 360 square miles in area. Its surface lies 1,292 feet below the Mediterranean. Its bitter, buoyant waters, asphalt deposits, and bordering wilderness are described with the region's exploration history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocaesarea:
Diocaesarea is the later name of Sepphoris, a town the rabbis called Sippori, meaning the bird. Though absent from the Bible, it ranked among the largest towns of Galilee. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Gabinius set one of five provincial councils there in 56 before Christ. Herod the Great retook it in 39 before Christ, and rebels seized it again in the year 3.

Herod Antipas rebuilt the ruined town and named it for the emperor, giving it the name Diocaesarea. The entry also treats two other sees of the same name, one in Thrace and one in Egypt. Bishops from the fourth century onward fill out a story of a town known more from councils and lists than from ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dioclea:
Dioclea was a titular see in Phrygia, a land of Asia Minor. Ptolemy names Diocleia, likely the Greek dress of a native name, Dokela. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry proves its self-rule from coins struck under the emperor Elagabalus. It appears in the Synecdemus of Hierocles and in later lists of bishoprics as a see of Phrygia Pacatiana, whose chief city was Laodicea.

Only two bishops are known, one in 431 and one in 451. An inscription found near Doghla, a village in the region of Smyrna, points to the site of Dioclea, though no ruins remain. The entry is a small study in how coins, lists, and a single stone can fix a lost bishopric on the map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elaea:
Elaea was an ancient port city of Asia Minor, now only a titular see, said to have been founded by Menestheus. It stood twelve stadia from the mouth of the Caicus river and one hundred and twenty stadia from Pergamus. It was the port of Pergamus. It enters history about 450 before Christ, in the days of the Athenian naval league. It passed from Alexander to the kings of Pergamus.

Antiochus of Syria besieged it in 190 before Christ, Prusias ravaged its land in 156, and an earthquake partly wrecked it in the year 90. In Roman times it struck its own coins. As a suffragan of Ephesus it appears in church lists to the twelfth or thirteenth century. Only three of its bishops are known: Isaias in 451, Olbianus in 787, and Theodulus in the twelfth century. Its ruins lie a few kilometres south of Kilisee Keui. Mongols or Turks likely destroyed the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-euroea:
Euroea was a small ancient see of Epirus Vetus in Greece, suffragan to the metropolitan of Nicopolis, now carried as a titular bishopric. The geographer Hierocles names it, and the emperor Justinian moved its people to an islet in a nearby lake and built a strong city there. Only five of its bishops are known, a thin record that still sketches a long life. The first, Saint Donatus, lived under Theodosius I, and the last appears in a letter of Pope Saint Gregory the Great written about 603.

The site itself is lost, and the entry weighs the guesses of scholars. Lequien placed it at Paramythia, called Aï Donal, or Saint Donatus, by the Turks, in the region of Janina. Others put it at Limboni, since shown to be Photice, or at Janina itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-c:
Eusebius of Caesarea, called the Father of Church History, was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century, born about 260 and dead before 341. The entry builds his life from his own letter to his diocese explaining why he signed the Creed of Nicaea. It weighs rival readings of that letter. One view holds that the creed he offered was the local creed of Caesarea, learned at his baptism and taught through his priesthood. 

The bulk of the article is a guide to his books. It covers his Church History, his apologetic works answering pagan and Jewish critics, and his commentaries on Scripture. It also covers his writings on doctrine, his orations, and his letters. It judges his strengths and limits as a historian, his part in the Arian dispute, and his standing at the court of Constantine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-l:
Eusebius of Laodicea was a third-century Alexandrian deacon who became bishop of Laodicea in Syria and died about 268. His story comes from Eusebius of Caesarea's Church History. As a deacon he stood with his bishop Dionysius before Aemilian, prefect of Egypt, under the emperor Valerian. All were sentenced to banishment. Eusebius stayed behind in hiding, served confessors in prison at great risk, and buried the bodies of martyrs.

When revolt and plague struck Alexandria in 260, he nursed the sick and wounded. He then won leave from the Roman general besieging the Bruchium quarter for all who wished to leave, and he tended the exhausted refugees like a father and physician. In 264 Dionysius sent him to Syria as his delegate in the affair of Paul of Samosata. The Syrians, impressed by him and his friend Anatolius, kept them both, making Eusebius bishop of Laodicea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-council:
The First Council of Nicaea met in 325 to meet the heresy of Arius. Constantine, now sole emperor, called bishops from every country to restore religious peace. The emperor supplied transport and upkeep, and opened the sessions with great solemnity. Some 318 bishops attended, most of them Greek, with Hosius of Cordova presiding.

The council condemned Arianism and framed the Nicene Creed, drawn up on 19 June. It also dealt with the paschal controversy and other matters before closing. The young deacon Athanasius was present, at the start of a life of conflict and glory. Sessions closed on 25 August, after the symbol and the remaining business were settled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederic-naus:
Frederic Nausea, bishop of Vienna, was a wagonmaker's son from Franconia who rose through learning to the Council of Trent. Born around 1480, he studied at Bamberg, Pavia, Padua, and Siena, taking degrees in law and divinity, then served Cardinal Campeggio as secretary at diets across Germany. Driven from Frankfurt by Lutheran riots, he preached at Mainz and became court preacher to King Ferdinand.

Named coadjutor of Vienna in 1538 and bishop in 1541, Nausea worked for reunion with the Lutherans, even asking Rome to allow married clergy and the communion cup for the laity. He reached Trent only in 1551, spoke chiefly on the sacraments, and died there of fever within the year. His writings range from sermons and a catechism to a treatise on the resurrection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-d-an:
Giovanni d'Andrea was a canonist born at Mugello near Florence about 1275, who died in 1348. Educated by his father and at the University of Bologna, he taught canon law at Padua and Pisa before becoming a professor at Bologna. His teaching ran for forty-five years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sums his career in his epitaph: Rabbi Doctorum, light, censor, and rule of morals.

Trithemius, Baldus, Forster, and Bellarmine paid him the highest tributes. He died in the plague of 1348, and was buried, the article says, in San Domenico at Bologna. His works include glosses on the sixth book of decretals and on the Clementines, a commentary on Gregory IX's decretals, and additions to the Speculum of Durandus. Later writers honored his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heraclea:
Heraclea, a titular see of Thracia Prima, was the name given some four centuries before Christ to Perinthus. It was an ancient Samian colony shaped like an amphitheatre on a peninsula in the Sea of Marmora. Famous for resisting Philip of Macedonia, it prospered as a port at the junction of great sea routes. Justinian repaired its aqueducts and a palace. It survives as Eregli in the vilayet of Adrianople, with ruins on a cape nearby.

Heraclea gained see status early, by Greek tradition from apostolic times, and once counted the Bishop of Byzantium under its jurisdiction. Its suffragans rose from five to seventeen, then fell to two in modern days, Myriophyton and Metrae. Its metropolitan, titled Exarch of Thrace and Macedonia and resident at Rodosto, hands the new Patriarch of Constantinople his crozier. Lequien lists forty-eight titulars, from martyrs and Arians to patriarchs of Constantinople.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hierocaesarea: Hierocaesarea was a titular see of Lydia, suffragan to Sardis, mentioned by Ptolemy and known from its coins to have worshipped Artemis Persica. Its site lay between the villages of Beyova and Sasova, south-east of Thyatira on the Koum-Chai, a tributary of the Hermus. It appears as a bishopric in the lists of sees until the twelfth or thirteenth century, with only three bishops known: Cosinius, Zacharias, and Theodore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idea:
Idea is a philosophical term carrying more shades of meaning than perhaps any other, yet its sense often holds the key to a philosopher's whole system. From Descartes onward usage grew confused and inconstant, and Locke, above all, ruined the term in English writing, where it ceased to hold any fixed meaning. Locke himself calls idea whatever the understanding takes as its object when a person thinks.

For Locke it covers, indifferently, a sensation, a perception, an imagined image, and an intellectual concept. It can also mean an emotional feeling, or the external material object perceived or imagined. The entry traces the word from its Greek root, to see, through ancient, medieval, and modern philosophy. It shows how one word came to bear so many loads and why its history matters for reading philosophers fairly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idumea:
Idumea is the country of Edom's descendants, its name the Greek form of Hebrew Edom, apparently from the red colour of its sandstone cliffs. It lay south of Juda and the Dead Sea, though its wilderness borders are hard to fix. Genesis says Esau settled on Mount Seir, then home of the Horites, after leaving Canaan.

Mount Seir is commonly identified with Jebel esh-Shera, prolonging Moab's mountains east of the Arabah. Yet signs point to a more westerly site in the highlands between Cades and the Dead Sea's southern end. The Amarna tablets name She-e-ri south of western Palestine and a city of Edom there. The entry traces Idumea's shifting bounds, peoples, and history from Esau's settlement onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ivrea:
Ivrea, a suffragan see of Turin in northern Italy, stands beside the Dora Baltea river and looks out finely toward the Great St Bernard. It started as a town of the Salassi people, Rome set a colony there in 90 before Christ, and in Lombard times it grew into the seat of a dukedom.

In 870 Emperor Guy of Spoleto handed the Mark of Ivrea to his brother Anscarius, whose heirs, Berengarius II and Arduinus, chased Italy's kingship. Afterward Ivrea battled for communal freedom against the marquesses of Monferrat, and in 1248 Frederick II handed it to Savoy's count. French troops laid siege to it and took it in 1554, 1641, 1704, and 1796.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-dawson-g:
John Dawson Gilmary Shea was an American historian who pioneered the study of early Catholic missions and exploration in America. Born in New York in 1824, he learned Spanish as a clerk in a Spanish merchant's office. He published at fourteen and studied law. He entered the Jesuits at Fordham in 1847, leaving the order in 1852 under the scholarly influence of Father Martin at Montreal.

He then began systematic research into early Indian missions. He published the Discovery and Exploration of the Mississippi Valley in 1852 with original narratives of Marquette, Allouez, and Hennepin. The Westminster Review and the Athenaeum praised it. His History of the Catholic Missions among the Indian Tribes followed in 1854. His Cramoisy Series republished rare pamphlets on early voyages, while his Library of American Linguistics gathered grammars and dictionaries of Indian languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-maria-de:
José María de Zalvidea was a Spanish Franciscan who spent four decades as a missionary in California, from 1805 until his death in 1846. Born in Bilbao in 1780, he joined the order in 1798 and passed through the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico. He then served in turn at San Fernando, San Gabriel, San Juan Capistrano, and San Luis Rey.

He was known as a model friar and a shrewd manager of mission lands and goods. Under his care Mission San Gabriel reached its peak of prosperity, and he joined a 1806 expedition seeking new mission sites while baptizing the dying along the way. The entry also notes his skill in Indian languages and his refusal to swear a political oath he saw as meddling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-of-ari:
Joseph of Arimathea was the wealthy Jew who buried Jesus after the Crucifixion. All certain knowledge of him comes from the Gospels. A member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish supreme council, and a secret disciple who had not agreed to Jesus' condemnation, he was a good and just man awaiting the kingdom of God.

After the Crucifixion, Joseph boldly asked Pilate for Jesus' body. With Nicodemus, who brought spices, he wrapped the body in linen and laid it in his own new rock tomb in a garden, rolling a great stone across the entrance. Later legends of his voyage to Gaul and Glastonbury, the entry warns, are fabulous and unworthy of credence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judea:
Judea was the Jewish homeland around Jerusalem after the return from captivity. Its name comes from the Aramaic Yehudai, and its first bounds ran from Bethsur in the south to Bethoron in the north, Emmaus in the west, and the Jordan in the east. Jews scattered elsewhere did not live in Judea proper.

The entry follows Judea from a Persian province through Alexander, Egypt, and Syria to Maccabean independence from 130 to 63 BC, then Roman tribute under Pompey. Under Herod, Christ was born at Bethlehem, and under Roman procurators, Pilate condemned him and Felix and Festus handled Paul. Its history is often confused with Jerusalem's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lady-elizabet:
Lady Elizabeth Herbert of Lea (1822-1911) was an author and philanthropist, daughter of General Charles A'Court, a soldier and member of Parliament. At twenty-four she married Sidney Herbert, a rising young politician and later Secretary of War in the Crimean campaign, when she worked closely with Florence Nightingale.

Widowed in 1861 with four sons and three daughters, she converted to Catholicism at Palermo in 1866, largely through Manning's influence, though only one child followed her. From then she led Catholic charities and poured out books, original and translated, that sold readily. Best known are Impressions of Spain, Cradle Lands on Egypt and Palestine, Wives and Mothers of the Olden Time, and Wayside Tales, plus lives of saints and statesmen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laodicea:
Laodicea was a titular see of Asia Minor, metropolis of Phrygia Pacatiana, first called Diospolis and Rhoas, then renamed by Antiochus II between 261 and 246 before Christ for his wife Laodice. It stood on a spur of Mount Salbacus near the Lycus river.

Achaeus ruled it in 220 before Christ, Pergamus held it next, and Mithridates' war battered it before Rome restored its prosperity. By the first century before Christ it ranked among Asia Minor's chief cities for woollen cloth and sandals, a free city and centre of a judicial district of twenty-four towns. Wealthy citizens raised fine monuments, a medical school flourished, and sceptic philosophers Antiochus and Theiodas were born there. Mongol and Turkish invasions later ruined it, leaving a stadium, theatres, and aqueduct near Denizli.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leonard-alea:
Leonard Alea was a French polemical writer of the early nineteenth century. Born in Paris at an unknown date and dead by 1812, he was from a family of bankers. In 1801 he published anonymously his first book, L'antidote de l'atheisme. The next year a new edition, enlarged to two volumes, appeared under a new title, La religion triomphante des attentats de l'impiete, bearing his name.

The book answered Sylvien Marechal's Dictionnaire des Athees, lately published, and its timely, fair, and pointed reply won a warm welcome. Marechal himself praised his adversary's moderation. Cardinal Gerdil praised the work highly. Portalis, to whom Alea dedicated the second edition, was delighted and later tried in vain to bring him into the Council of State. Alea's only other work is Reflexions contre le divorce, also of 1802.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorea: Lorea was a titular see in the Roman province of Arabia, a lesser bishopric under Bostra. Its city shows up only in tenth-century lists of bishops under Antioch, spelled Lourea, Dourea, and Lorea in different manuscripts. No geographer names it, its site is unknown, and nothing more is recorded of it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-medea:
Medea, a titular see of Thrace under Heraclea, takes its name, like modern Midieh, from ancient Salmydessos or Alydessos. Herodotus says its people yielded to Darius after some resistance, and Xenophon with his men subdued it only with great trouble. Sophocles, Aeschylus, Diodorus, Strabo, and Ptolemy all place its harbour on the Black Sea, open to winds, with a sandy shore bad for ships. Aeschylus wrongly sets it in Asia.

Theophanes names it Medeia in 763. Emperor John Cantacuzenus took it in 1352 and nearly died there at Turkish hands. It appears as a suffragan of Heraclea about 900 in Leo the Wise's Notitia, and again under Manuel Comnenus about 1170 and Michael VIII about 1270. Under Andronicus II it became an autocephalous archbishopric, and about 1330 a metropolitan see. The entry follows the town from classical port to Byzantine church centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neocaesarea:
Pontus Polemoniacus holds Neocaesarea as a titular see, though Cabira was its first name. Mithridates the Great favoured the place as a home and raised a palace on the spot; King Polemon and those who followed him favoured it too. Pompey gave it city rank under the name Diopolis. Polemon's widow Pythodoris then chose it for her capital, calling it Sebaste. By the day of Pliny it bore the name Neocaesarea, a change its coins suggest fell under Tiberius.

The city grew into the civil and religious centre of Pontus. Gregory Thaumaturgus, a native son, took up its bishopric around 240, when only seventeen Christians lived there; by his death in 270, only seventeen pagans remained. A great council gathered there in 315, and its acts survive. Quakes levelled the city in 344 and again in 499. Through the Middle Ages Muslims and Christians fought over it, until Ottoman rule began in 1397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-guinea:
New Guinea, the world's second largest island and one of its least known countries, lies immediately north of Australia. It stretches from the equator to about 12 degrees south and 130 to 154 degrees east. It is 1,490 miles long, up to 430 miles broad, covering some 310,000 square miles, with a purely conjectural population of 875,000. D'Abreu, long credited with its discovery in 1511, reached only Further India's eastern coast.

Whether Menzes, Saavedra and Grijalva reached it remains uncertain, but Ortiz de Retas landed in 1545 at the Saint Augustine River's mouth, took possession for Spain, and named it Nueva Guinea. Torres in 1606 first circumnavigated most of the island, and Tasman, Vuik and Kayto mapped southern and eastern coasts. The entry follows later exploration, the island's peoples and geography, and the Catholic missions dividing its coasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicaea:
Nicaea, a titular see of Bithynia Secunda on Lake Ascanius in a fertile but summer-unhealthful plain, was first colonised by the Battaei as Ancora or Helicora. Destroyed by Mysians, Antigonus rebuilt it about 315 BC after beating Eumenius and called it Antigonia. Lysimachus later enlarged it and named it Nicaea for his wife.

Bithynian kings resided there almost as often as at Nicomedia, with which it struggled for influence. It was the birthplace of astronomer Hipparchus and historian Dio Cassius, and Pliny the Younger often mentions its monuments. After the first Ecumenical Council in 325, Constantine titled it metropolis, which Valens withdrew but it kept ecclesiastically. It took suffragans from Nicomedia, and in 787 hosted the second Ecumenical Council, the seventh, against Iconoclasts, with over 300 bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicotera-and-:
Nicotera and Tropea, a united diocese in Calabria, joins two coastal towns battered by earthquake and Turkish raids. Nicotera, ancient Medama, was wrecked in 1783, and its first known bishop, Proculus, received a letter from Gregory the Great in 599.

Tropea, perched on a reef in the Gulf of Saint Euphemia, gave birth to the painter Spanò and the philosopher Pasquale Galluppi, and its cathedral rose again after 1783. United in 1818, the diocese counts 72 parishes and 78,000 inhabitants, with Franciscan and Sisters of Charity houses. Bishop Charles Pinti saw the city pillaged by the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamphilus-of-:
Pamphilus of Caesarea, martyred in 309, gave his name to one of the great early Christian libraries. Eusebius's life of him is lost, but his Martyrs of Palestine tells that Pamphilus came of a noble Beirut family, sold all he owned for the poor, and joined the perfect men. At Alexandria his teacher Pierius headed the famed catechetical school, and Photius drew on Pamphilus's Apology for Origen.

Settled at Caesarea, Pamphilus was ordained priest, gathered his famous library, and opened a school of theological study. His chief labour was making accurate copies of Scripture, praised in manuscript colophons. Jerome says he copied most of Origen's works with his own hand, and kept twenty-five volumes of Origen commentaries copied by Pamphilus as a precious relic. Eusebius catalogued the library in his lost life of the martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-de-vine:
Peter de Vinea was the chief minister of Emperor Frederick II, born at Capua about 1190. Legal learning and elegant Latin carried him to the top of the imperial court, where he strengthened Frederick's drive toward absolute rule in Church and State. As chief judge he shaped justice and law in Sicily, and he probably helped draft the Constitutions of Melfi issued in 1231.

By 1247 he stood alone at the head of the imperial chancery as prothonotary and logothete of Sicily. The height proved his ruin. He enriched himself and his kin until, by the emperor's own account, his thefts threatened the empire's finances. Suspected also in a plot to poison Frederick at Cremona in February 1249, he fell from favour and died that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-procopius-of-:
Procopius of Caesarea, Byzantine historian, was born in the fifth century's late years at Caesarea in Palestine and died no earlier than 562. No word survives of his parentage or schooling, save that legal training fitted him for the civil service. Ere Justin died, in 527 at the earliest, he joined Belisarius as counsellor, assessor, and secretary, following his fortunes and campaigns for twelve or fifteen years.
